items.prose: A running club has 9 sprinters. It picks a relay team of 4 and then a running order for the 4 legs. Every team, and every order of a team, is equally likely. Ada and Bea are the two fastest sprinters.

parts.question: How many different teams of 4, ignoring the running order, can the club pick?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Swapping two sprinters gives the same team.

byKey.ordered: That counts ordered picks, $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6$. A team is the same 4 sprinters whatever the order.
byKey.times: You multiplied 9 by 4. Count the ordered picks, then divide by the $4!$ orders of each team.

explain.text: There are $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 3024$ ordered picks. Each team appears once per order of its members, $4! = 24$ times, so there are $\tfrac{3024}{24} = 126$ teams.

parts.question: Using the 126 teams, how many line-ups are there: a team together with its running order?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each team can run in $4!$ orders.

byKey.times-four: You multiplied by 4. A team of 4 can run in $4! = 24$ orders.
byKey.added: You added the 24 orders. Each team pairs with each of its orders, so multiply.

explain.text: Each of the 126 teams runs in $4! = 24$ orders, so there are $126 \times 24 = 3024$ line-ups. That matches $9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6$, filling the legs one at a time.

parts.question: Using the 126 teams, what is the chance that both Ada and Bea are in the team? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Teams with both fill the other 2 places from 7: $\binom{7}{2} = 21$, and $\tfrac{21}{126} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put Ada and Bea in, then count the ways to fill the other places.

byKey.one-named: That is $\tfrac{4}{9}$, the chance one named sprinter is in. Both must be in.
byKey.squared: That is $\left(\tfrac{4}{9}\right)^2$, which treats the two picks as independent. Once Ada is in, only 3 places are left for 8 sprinters.

explain.text: With Ada and Bea in, the other 2 places come from the other 7 sprinters: $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ teams. So the chance is $\tfrac{21}{126} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.

parts.question: Using $P(\text{both in}) = \tfrac{1}{6}$, what is the chance that Ada and Bea run the last two legs, in either order? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Given both are in, they take legs 3 and 4 in $2 \times 2$ of the 24 orders: $\tfrac{1}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{1}{36}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take a team holding both. Count its orders with Ada and Bea on legs 3 and 4.

byKey.one-order: That is $\tfrac{1}{72}$, with Bea on the last leg only. Either order counts, so double it.
byKey.in-team: That is the chance both are in the team. They must also take legs 3 and 4.
byKey.from-squared: That is $\left(\tfrac{4}{9}\right)^2 \times \tfrac{1}{6}$, from the independent picks of part 3. Use $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

explain.text: In a team holding both, Ada and Bea take legs 3 and 4 in 2 ways. The others take legs 1 and 2 in 2 ways: 4 of 24 orders. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{6} \times \tfrac{4}{24} = \tfrac{1}{36}$, or $\tfrac{84}{3024}$ line-ups.

items.prose: A batch holds 15 orders, and 4 of them breach a risk limit. A checker picks 3 different orders from the batch at random, one after another, without replacement.

parts.question: What is the chance that the first order picked does not breach? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the orders that do not breach.

byKey.breach: That is $\tfrac{4}{15}$, the chance it does breach.

explain.text: Of 15 orders, $15 - 4 = 11$ are clean. The first pick is equally likely to be any order, so the chance is $\tfrac{11}{15}$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{11}{15}$ for the first pick, what is the chance that the first two orders are both clean? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. After a clean first pick, how many orders and how many clean ones are left?

byKey.replace: That is $\left(\tfrac{11}{15}\right)^2$, as if the first order went back. It stays out, so 14 are left.
byKey.fixed-bottom: You took one clean order off the top but kept 15 on the bottom. The batch has 14 left.
byKey.fixed-top: You took one order off the bottom but kept 11 clean on the top. Only 10 clean ones are left.

explain.text: After a clean first pick, 14 orders are left and 10 of them are clean. Multiply along the branch: $\tfrac{11}{15} \times \tfrac{10}{14} = \tfrac{11}{21} \approx 0.5238$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{11}{21}$ for the first two, what is the chance that all three orders are clean? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. After two clean picks, 13 orders are left and 9 of them are clean.

byKey.replace: That is $\left(\tfrac{11}{15}\right)^3$, drawing with replacement. Each pick leaves one order fewer.
byKey.fixed-bottom: That is $\tfrac{11 \times 10 \times 9}{15^3}$, with 15 kept on the bottom. The batch shrinks too.

explain.text: After two clean picks, 13 orders are left, 9 of them clean. So the chance is $\tfrac{11}{21} \times \tfrac{9}{13} = \tfrac{33}{91} \approx 0.3626$.

parts.question: Using $P(\text{all clean}) = \tfrac{33}{91}$, what is the chance the checker finds at least one breach? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. “At least one breach” is the complement of “all clean”.

byKey.none: That is the chance of no breach. Take it from 1.
byKey.replace: That is $1 - \left(\tfrac{11}{15}\right)^3$, with replacement. Without replacement the chance is higher.
byKey.adding: That is $3 \times \tfrac{4}{15}$, which adds a chance per pick. Samples with two breaches are counted twice.

explain.text: “At least one breach” is the complement of “all three clean”. So the chance is $1 - \tfrac{33}{91} = \tfrac{58}{91} \approx 0.6374$.

parts.question: The checker may keep picking, still without replacement. Three clean picks have chance $\tfrac{33}{91}$. What is the smallest number of picks for which at least one breach has chance above 0.9?

feedback.correct: Each pick multiplies by the clean orders left over the orders left. The breach chance is 0.7582 at 4 picks, 0.8462 at 5 and 0.9077 at 6. So 6 is the first above 0.9.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply $\tfrac{33}{91}$ by $\tfrac{8}{12}$, then $\tfrac{7}{11}$, and so on, and watch the chance of a breach.

byKey.five: At 5 picks the chance of at least one breach is 0.8462, still under 0.9.
byKey.adding: That solves $\tfrac{4n}{15} > 0.9$, which adds a chance per pick. At 4 picks the true chance is 0.7582.
byKey.replace: That is the answer if each order went back after the pick. Without replacement the clean orders run out faster, so fewer picks are needed.

explain.text: After the three picks, each further pick multiplies the all-clean chance by $\tfrac{8}{12}$, $\tfrac{7}{11}$ and $\tfrac{6}{10}$ in turn: $0.2418$, $0.1538$, then $0.0923$. So the breach chance is 0.7582, 0.8462 and 0.9077 at 4, 5 and 6 picks. The direct count agrees at 6: $1 - \tfrac{\binom{11}{6}}{\binom{15}{6}} = 1 - \tfrac{462}{5005}$.

items.prose: Eight members of a pricing committee each cast one vote for one of three proposals, X, Y and Z. Only the tally is published: how many votes each proposal got, such as 3, 3 and 2.

parts.question: How many different tallies are possible?

feedback.correct: A tally is a row of 8 votes and 2 bars: $\binom{10}{2} = 45$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Code a tally as 8 stars and 2 bars.

byKey.distinct: That is $3^8$, which lists who voted for what. The tally keeps only the counts, so the votes act as identical.
byKey.at-least-one: That is $\binom{7}{2}$, with every proposal getting a vote. A proposal may get none.
byKey.stars-only: You put the 2 bars among 8 places. The row has $8 + 2 = 10$ places.

explain.text: A tally shares 8 identical votes among 3 proposals. That is a row of 8 stars and 2 bars, so there are $\binom{8 + 2}{2} = \binom{10}{2} = 45$ tallies.

parts.question: Using the 45 tallies, how many leave at least one proposal with no votes?

feedback.correct: Every proposal gets a vote in $\binom{7}{2} = 21$ tallies, so $45 - 21 = 24$ leave one empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the tallies where every proposal gets a vote, then use the complement.

byKey.all-voted: That is $\binom{7}{2}$, the tallies where every proposal gets a vote. Take it from 45.
byKey.unanimous: Those are the tallies with two empty proposals. Tallies such as 5, 3, 0 have one empty proposal.

explain.text: With at least one vote each, the 2 bars go in the 7 gaps between the votes: $\binom{7}{2} = 21$. The complement holds $45 - 21 = 24$ tallies.

parts.question: Each member now votes independently, choosing each proposal with chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Are the 45 tallies equally likely?

options.text: No. The tally 3, 3, 2 comes from many lists of votes; 8, 0, 0 comes from only one.
Yes. Each tally has chance $\tfrac{1}{45}$ because the proposals are alike.
options.why: You gave every tally the same chance. The equally likely outcomes are the $3^8$ lists of votes, and a tally can hold many lists.

options.text: Yes. The votes are identical, so each sharing is one outcome.
options.why: Identical votes make tallies the right thing to count, not equally likely things to count. Members are different people.

options.text: No. The tally 8, 0, 0 is the most likely, since members agree.
options.why: You assumed the members agree. Each votes independently, so a split tally holds far more vote lists.

feedback.correct: The equally likely outcomes are the $3^8$ lists of who voted for what. A tally such as 3, 3, 2 holds many of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how many lists of votes give each tally.

explain.text: Each member has 3 equally likely choices, so the $3^8 = 6561$ vote lists are the equally likely outcomes. Only one list gives 8, 0, 0, while 3, 3, 2 comes from hundreds. So the tallies are not equally likely.

parts.question: Using the $3^8 = 6561$ equally likely vote lists, what is the chance the vote is unanimous, all 8 for one proposal? Give a fraction or a decimal to 6 places.

feedback.correct: Three vote lists are unanimous, one for each proposal: $\tfrac{3}{6561} = \tfrac{1}{2187}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the vote lists in which all 8 votes match.

byKey.tallies: That is $\tfrac{3}{45}$, treating the 45 tallies as equally likely. Part 3 showed they are not.
byKey.one-proposal: That is $\tfrac{1}{6561}$, all 8 for X only. Y and Z can be unanimous too.

explain.text: A unanimous vote is all X, all Y or all Z: 3 of the 6561 lists. So the chance is $\tfrac{3}{6561} = \tfrac{1}{2187} \approx 0.000457$, far below the $\tfrac{3}{45}$ that equal tallies would give.

items.prose: A data vendor runs 30 feeds. Each quarter an audit picks 5 different feeds at random, every set of 5 equally likely, independently of other quarters. Your team runs 5 of the 30 feeds.

parts.question: How many different sets of 5 feeds can the audit pick?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count ordered picks without repeats, then divide by the orders of a set.

byKey.ordered: That is $30 \times 29 \times 28 \times 27 \times 26$, ordered picks. Divide by the $5!$ orders of each set.
byKey.power: That is $30^5$, picks with repeats in order. The audit picks 5 different feeds, as a set.

explain.text: There are $30 \times 29 \times 28 \times 27 \times 26 = 17{,}100{,}720$ ordered picks. Each set of 5 appears $5! = 120$ times, so there are 142,506 sets.

parts.question: Using the 142,506 sets, what is the chance that exactly 3 of the audited feeds are your team's? Give a decimal to 5 places.

feedback.correct: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ ways for your 3 and $\binom{25}{2} = 300$ for the other 2: $\tfrac{3000}{142{,}506} \approx 0.02105$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose 3 of your 5 feeds, then 2 of the other 25, and multiply.

byKey.no-others: That is $\tfrac{10}{142{,}506}$, which picks your 3 feeds but not the other 2. Multiply by $\binom{25}{2} = 300$.
byKey.others-ordered: You picked the other 2 feeds in order, $25 \times 24$. They form a set, so halve it: 300.

explain.text: In stages: choose 3 of your 5 feeds, $\binom{5}{3} = 10$, then 2 of the other 25, $\binom{25}{2} = 300$. That gives 3000 sets, so the chance is $\tfrac{3000}{142{,}506} \approx 0.02105$.

parts.question: Using the 3000 sets with exactly 3, find the chance that at least 3 audited feeds are yours. Give a decimal to 5 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. “At least 3” is exactly 3, 4 or 5 of your feeds.

byKey.exactly: That is the chance of exactly 3. Add the sets with 4 and with 5 of yours.
byKey.double-four: You counted the 4-feed sets as $\binom{5}{4} \times \binom{25}{1} \times 2 = 250$. There are 125 of them.

explain.text: Exactly 4 of yours gives $\binom{5}{4}\binom{25}{1} = 125$ sets and exactly 5 gives 1. These are disjoint, so the chance is $\tfrac{3000 + 125 + 1}{142{,}506} = \tfrac{3126}{142{,}506} \approx 0.02194$.

parts.question: Let $p \approx 0.021936$ be the chance of at least 3 of yours in a quarter, from part 3. Find the chance this happens in at least one of the next 4 quarters. Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance it happens in no quarter, then take it from 1.

byKey.adding: That is $4 \times 0.021936$, which adds a chance per quarter. Runs with two such quarters are counted twice.
byKey.from-exactly: That is $1 - (1 - 0.021052)^4$, from the exactly 3 chance. Use the at least 3 chance from part 3.
byKey.none: That is $(1 - 0.021936)^4$, the chance it never happens. Take it from 1.

explain.text: The quarters are independent, so it happens in none with chance $(1 - 0.021936)^4 \approx 0.91510$. The complement gives $1 - 0.91510 \approx 0.0849$.
